content: The World Bank classifies economies into income groups (low, lower-middle, upper-middle, and high) based on gross national income (GNI) per capita, calculated using the World Bank Atlas method. For the fiscal year 2024, low-income economies are defined as those with a GNI per capita of $1,135 or less in 2022. Lower-middle-income economies have a GNI per capita between $1,136 and $4,465, upper-middle-income economies range from $4,466 to $13,845, and high-income economies are those with a GNI per capita of $13,846 or more. Maximal sterile barrier precautions involve the use of a cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, and a sterile full-body drape to minimize infection risks during medical procedures. Multimodal improvement strategies (MMIS) are designed to enhance the implementation of interventions by addressing systemic, behavioral, and environmental factors to achieve measurable improvements. These strategies often include tools like bundles and checklists, developed by multidisciplinary teams that consider local conditions. MMIS emphasizes a comprehensive approach, targeting multiple factors influencing human behavior rather than relying solely on single strategies like education or training. The five key components of MMIS are system change (Build it), training and education (Teach it), monitoring and feedback (Check it), reminders and communication (Sell it), and culture change (Live it). These elements are tailored to the local healthcare context and informed by periodic assessments. Sterile technique refers to a set of practices aimed at eliminating all microorganisms from equipment and areas to maintain sterility. This is particularly critical for procedures like inserting peripheral arterial catheters (PACs) and peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs). The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence of the World Health Organization (WHO) Guideline Development Group (GDG) in the balance between the benefits and risks of implementing a recommendation. Strong recommendations are issued when the GDG is confident that the benefits outweigh the risks, while conditional (or weak) recommendations are made when there is uncertainty about this balance. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), including bloodstream infections (BSIs) and antimicrobial-resistant infections, pose a significant burden globally, harming patients across all income levels. BSIs associated with intravascular catheters are among the most preventable infections if proper precautions are followed during catheter insertion, maintenance, access, and removal. Intravascular catheters are broadly categorized into those inserted into peripheral blood vessels (veins and arteries) and those inserted into central vessels. Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are the most commonly used invasive devices in healthcare, with up to 70% of inpatients requiring one during their hospital stay. This widespread use highlights the potential global burden of PIVC-associated BSIs and related infections. PICCs, while less frequently used than PIVCs, carry a higher risk of systemic BSIs due to their placement in large central veins. The WHO guidelines for preventing infections associated with intravenous (IV) catheters provide evidence-based recommendations for best practices in managing peripheral IV catheters, including PIVCs, PICCs, and PACs. The recommendations emphasize education, hand hygiene, sterile techniques, and multimodal strategies to minimize infection risks. For example, clinicians are advised to use sterile gloves and standardized insertion kits for catheter placement and to follow formal sterile dressing protocols for catheter maintenance. The guidelines also suggest using ultrasound guidance for PICC insertion and prioritizing upper limb veins over lower limb veins for PIVC placement. Regular assessment of catheter sites for signs of infection and timely removal of catheters inserted under emergency conditions are also recommended. The development of these guidelines followed a rigorous process, including systematic reviews of scientific evidence, stakeholder consultations, and the application of the GRADE framework to evaluate the balance of benefits and risks. The guidelines are structured into six key sections: education and hand hygiene, insertion, maintenance, access, removal, and catheter choice. They include 14 good practice statements and 23 recommendations, emphasizing the importance of multimodal strategies and clinical care bundles to improve outcomes. The WHO strongly advocates for the implementation of these strategies to reduce the global burden of catheter-associated BSIs and related infections, regardless of a country's income level.
